title: Sunflowers (Van Gogh Museum version)

image.credit: Van Gogh Museum, Netherlands; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A vase of sunflowers painted in many shades of yellow and orange, set against a yellow background. The paint is thick, with visible, energetic brushstrokes.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting on canvas by Vincent van Gogh, dated 1888 by the source page, in the Van Gogh Museum in the Netherlands. Van Gogh painted more than one sunflower still life, so this is one of several related pictures.

descriptions.k: Look at all this yellow! Sunflowers sit in a vase. Some are big and some are small. The paint looks thick and bumpy. Which sunflower do you like best?
descriptions.g12: Vincent van Gogh painted these sunflowers in 1888. He used thick paint and lots of yellow. Look at the petals and the middle of each flower. How many shades of yellow can you find? What mood do they give you?
descriptions.g35: Vincent van Gogh painted Sunflowers in 1888 using thick oil paint. Almost everything in the picture is yellow, but he found many different shades. Look at the flower heads, the vase and the table. How does Van Gogh keep so much yellow interesting, and what mood does it create?
descriptions.g68: Van Gogh's Sunflowers (1888) is a Post-Impressionist still life painted almost entirely in yellows. Thick, visible brushstrokes make the petals feel alive, and each flower is at a different stage, some open and some past their best. How do color and brushwork express feeling, and what do the flowers' different stages add?
descriptions.g910: Van Gogh's Sunflowers (1888) is a landmark of Post-Impressionism, building a still life from closely related yellows and thick, directional brushwork. The flowers appear at different stages, which some viewers connect to time and change. How do limited color and visible paint make a simple vase of flowers so intense?
descriptions.g1112: Van Gogh's Sunflowers (1888) shows how Post-Impressionism used a humble subject to test color, surface and feeling. The near-monochrome yellows and the heavy impasto make the picture both a still life and an assertion of painterly presence. Van Gogh made several related versions. How does repetition of a motif shape the way we think about originality and expression?

k.daily: Look at the sunflowers in the vase. Which one looks happiest, and why?
k.emotion: How does all this yellow make you feel?
k.observation: Count how many sunflowers you can find. Which one is biggest?
k.analysis: Which sunflower did your eyes find before the others, and what pulled you there?
k.line: Trace one petal with your finger. Is it curvy or pointy?
k.shape: Find a round shape in the middle of a sunflower. What does it remind you of?
k.color: How many different yellows can you find? Point to two that are not the same.
k.texture: The paint on the sunflowers looks heaped up. How would it feel under your fingertip?
k.space: Which flowers look closest to you, and which look farther back?
k.light: Where does the light shine on the flowers?
k.meaning: Why might a painter choose sunflowers to paint again and again?
k.culture: Sunflowers grow in many places. Have you ever seen one, and where was it?
k.technique: The artist used thick paint. What kind of brush do you think he used?
k.personal: If you painted flowers in only one color, which color would you choose?
k.critical: What would you change about the vase or the table?

g12.daily: Why do you think Van Gogh painted so many shades of yellow?
g12.emotion: What mood do the yellow petals and the bright background give you, and where is it strongest?
g12.observation: List five things you notice, from the flower centers to the petals and vase.
g12.analysis: How does the vase and the arrangement of flowers lead your eyes around the picture?
g12.line: Where do you see the curved lines of petals and the straight lines of stems?
g12.shape: Which shapes in the sunflowers repeat, and how do they make the picture feel steady?
g12.color: How do the different yellows make the flowers stand out from the background?
g12.texture: Where does the paint look thickest, and how does it make the flowers feel real?
g12.space: How close do the flowers feel, and what does the painter do to make them seem near?
g12.light: Where does the light seem to land on the flowers, and how can you tell?
g12.meaning: What might it mean that some sunflowers are open and others are drooping?
g12.culture: What can a painting of flowers from 1888 tell us about what mattered to the painter?
g12.technique: How is painting with thick, short strokes different from smooth blending?
g12.personal: Which flower in the painting would you pick to take home, and why?
g12.critical: What would you tell a friend who has never seen this painting?

g35.daily: How do the shapes of the petals and centers show different stages in the life of the flowers?
g35.emotion: What feeling do the yellows give you, and what details support your idea?
g35.observation: Study one flower closely. How does Van Gogh use brushstrokes to build its petals and center?
g35.analysis: How does the arrangement of the flowers in the vase balance the picture?
g35.line: Where do you see lines made by thick brushstrokes, and which way do they point?
g35.shape: How do the round flower heads and the tall vase shape the structure of the painting?
g35.color: How does Van Gogh keep so much yellow from looking boring? Name two choices.
g35.texture: How can you tell the paint was put on thickly, and what does that do to the surface?
g35.space: How does the artist make the sunflowers seem to come toward you?
g35.light: How does light help show the shapes of the flowers when almost everything is yellow?
g35.meaning: Why might Van Gogh have chosen sunflowers, and what might they mean to him or to viewers?
g35.culture: Sunflowers are grown in many parts of the world. What might a painter in 1888 think about when painting them?
g35.technique: What technique does Van Gogh use to give the flowers texture instead of smooth color?
g35.personal: What would you want to ask the painter about these flowers?
g35.critical: What makes a painting of flowers as serious a subject as a painting of people? Use details to explain.

g68.daily: How do the flowers' different stages and the thick paint work together to give the painting life?
g68.emotion: What emotions might the glowing yellows suggest, and how do individual details support or complicate them?
g68.observation: Compare how the flowers, vase and background are painted. What differences stand out?
g68.analysis: How does the composition hold the cluster of flowers together and keep them from feeling crowded?
g68.line: How do directional brushstrokes act as lines that give each petal a shape?
g68.shape: How do the repeated circular flower heads create rhythm across the picture?
g68.color: How might Van Gogh's use of nearly all yellow be an expressive choice rather than just a description?
g68.texture: What does the thick impasto reveal about how the painter worked and how it changes the way light hits the surface?
g68.space: How does the shallow space push the flowers toward the viewer?
g68.light: How is the light handled when the entire painting is made of warm colors?
g68.meaning: How might the presence of both fresh and fading flowers be read by different viewers?
g68.culture: How might the shift away from Impressionism in the late 1880s be visible in this painting?
g68.technique: How does impasto differ from thin, blended oil paint, and what effect does it have on the petals?
g68.personal: What does the painting make you feel about everyday objects as subjects for art?
g68.critical: How does limiting a painting mostly to yellows make it more powerful or more limited? Support your view with evidence.

g910.daily: How does a single dominant color serve the expressive aim of the painting?
g910.emotion: How do thick paint and glowing color create an emotional tone, and what role do the drooping flowers play?
g910.observation: Examine the junction of petals and background. What does the treatment reveal about Van Gogh's method?
g910.analysis: How does the arrangement of the flowers in the vase set up a hierarchy and balance?
g910.line: How do the directional strokes of impasto act as both line and texture?
g910.shape: How do circular flower heads and the cylindrical vase structure the composition?
g910.color: How does a range of closely related yellows create unity and variety?
g910.texture: What does the physical thickness of the paint imply about the picture as an object, not only an image?
g910.space: How does the compressed, nearly flat space affect the viewer's relationship to the flowers?
g910.light: How does the painter use light and dark within the yellow family to model the forms?
g910.meaning: How might the flowers at different stages suggest ideas about time, and what are the limits of that reading?
g910.culture: How does the painting reflect Post-Impressionism's shift toward subjective expression and away from fleeting optical effects?
g910.technique: How does Van Gogh's technique with thick oil paint differ from academic still life painting?
g910.personal: What does this painting make you consider about how an ordinary object can become extraordinary?
g910.critical: To what extent is the painting's fame bound up with its color, and to what extent with its subject? Argue from the image.

g1112.daily: How does the painting transform a modest still life into a statement about color and feeling?
g1112.emotion: How much of the picture's intensity comes from the flowers, the paint or the viewer's expectations? Weigh the visual evidence.
g1112.observation: Scan the edges where flowers meet ground. How does the near-monochrome palette challenge conventional rules about contrast?
g1112.analysis: How does the composition balance density and openness in a tightly packed arrangement?
g1112.line: In what ways do the directional marks serve both description and an independent, rhythmic energy?
g1112.shape: How might the repetition of circular forms reflect Post-Impressionist interest in structure beneath appearances?
g1112.color: How might the yellow-dominated palette be read as both observation and invention, and what limits our certainty?
g1112.texture: What is at stake in the visible, heavy paint surface for modern ideas of painting as object?
g1112.space: How does the confined, flattened space reposition the still life tradition?
g1112.light: How does the painting evoke light without relying on conventional modeling?
g1112.meaning: How do scholars navigate the temptation to read life into the flowers, and what does the image itself support?
g1112.culture: How does the existence of several related sunflower paintings complicate ideas about originality and the single masterpiece?
g1112.technique: How does Van Gogh's technique anticipate later modern painting, and how can you test that comparison against what you see?
g1112.personal: How does your own cultural sense of flowers shape what you read in this picture?
g1112.critical: What would a persuasive argument look like that the painting is more about painting than about flowers, and how would you counter it?

teacherNote.context: A flower still life in oil by Vincent van Gogh, dated 1888 by the source page, in the Van Gogh Museum. Van Gogh painted several related sunflower pictures.
directions: Have students paint or draw a flower using only shades of one color and compare their versions.
Ask students to find the flowers at different stages and tell the story of time passing.
Discuss why an artist might paint the same subject more than once.
